lessons.contracts__ijara:
In an ijara contract, what's being sold isn't the item itself — it's the right to use it, the manfaa. Ownership stays with the lessor, and that one fact drives everything else in the deal.

Because the lessor still owns the asset, they carry the owner's risks. If the item is destroyed through no fault of the renter — a leased delivery van totaled in an accident, say — the loss is the lessor's, and payments stop. Major repairs, insurance, the core costs of ownership: that's on the lessor. The renter is only responsible for routine upkeep and for damage caused by their own negligence.

This is exactly the line that separates a real lease from a loan wearing a lease costume. If the contract says the renter keeps paying no matter what — even after the asset is gone — then the risk was never really with the owner. Calling it a lease doesn't make it one.

This matters directly for anyone looking at ijara muntahia bittamlik — lease-to-own structures used as alternatives to a mortgage or car loan. Scholars insist that the transfer of ownership at the end has to be a separate promise (a gift or a sale), not built into the lease itself in a way that turns the rent payments into disguised installment payments. If the two get merged, you've effectively created an installment sale mislabeled as a lease — the same problem in different clothes.

Late-payment penalties charged as a percentage are not allowed in ijara, for the same reason they're not allowed in murabaha.

One more thing worth carrying with you, and it applies beyond equipment leases: this same category covers hiring people, not just renting things. There's a hadith where the Prophet ﷺ names three people he will personally stand against on the Day of Judgment — and one of them is someone who hired a worker, got the work done in full, and then didn't pay. If you employ staff, contract freelancers, or hire help for your business, the same principle applies: wages owed for work completed are not something to delay or shortchange.
lessons.contracts__mudaraba-musharaka:
Mudaraba and musharaka are the two partnership contracts that actually replace interest-based lending — because in both, profit is tied to risk. That link is the whole point.

**Mudaraba**: one side puts up the capital (the investor), the other runs the business (the manager). Profit is split by an agreed ratio — say 60/40. If the venture loses money, the investor loses the capital, and the manager loses their time and effort and walks away with nothing. But if the loss came from negligence or from breaking the agreed terms, the manager is on the hook for it.

**Musharaka**: both sides put in capital, and both can take part in running things. Profit can be split however you agree — it doesn't have to match the capital ratio, so a partner who also does the work can take a bigger cut. Loss, however, must be split strictly according to each partner's share of the capital. That part isn't negotiable.

Here's the rule that decides whether something is really a partnership or just a loan wearing a disguise: you can agree on a *share* of profit, but never on a *fixed amount*. The moment one side is guaranteed a set return regardless of outcome, the risk has been removed, and what you have is interest under another name — no matter what it's called. For the same reason, no partner can promise to return the other partner's capital in full.

For a mortgage-style need, there's **musharaka mutanaqisa** — diminishing partnership. The financier and the client buy a home together, say in a 20/80 split. The client lives in it and pays rent on the financier's share while also buying out that share bit by bit. As the financier's share shrinks, the rent shrinks with it, until the client owns the whole property. This is one of the main Islamic alternatives to a conventional mortgage — useful to know if you're comparing options against your current mortgage.

There's a hadith that captures why partnership carries real weight in this tradition: Allah says He is the third partner between two people in business, as long as neither betrays the other — and He withdraws the moment one does.
lessons.contracts__murabaha:
Murabaha is the contract you'll meet most often in Islamic finance — and the one most often misused.

The mechanics are straightforward. Instead of lending you money at interest, the financier buys the actual item — a car, equipment, inventory — takes ownership of it, then sells it to you at "cost plus markup," stated openly. You pay in installments.

Three conditions have to hold, or it's not really murabaha:

- **Real ownership first.** The financier has to actually buy the item and carry the risk of owning it before selling it to you. If it's destroyed between purchase and resale, that's the financier's loss, not yours. Skip this, and you're just selling something you never owned.
- **Open markup.** The whole point of murabaha is that cost and markup are stated plainly, not buried. A hidden markup invalidates the contract as murabaha.
- **Fixed price, one time.** The total is set once and doesn't grow because you're late. If it grows over time, riba has crept back in, whatever the contract is called.

Here's the honest part. If the financier's "ownership" lasts five minutes and exists only on paper, the end result looks exactly like an interest loan — and some scholars say so directly. That's why industry standards spell out in detail what real ownership has to look like, as opposed to formal ownership. How well practice actually matches the standard is a genuine, ongoing debate inside the industry — not something this lesson can settle for you.

So what happens if you're late on a payment, given that the price can't increase? In practice, a fixed, pre-agreed penalty is allowed — but it can't go into the financier's income. It's routed to charity instead. That keeps it a discipline tool, not a way to profit from someone's hardship. And the Quran itself is direct on this: if someone is in genuine difficulty, they're owed more time, not more debt.

If a contract you're offered doesn't clearly show these three things — the seller actually owning the asset first, the markup stated openly, and a price that's locked in regardless of delay — it's worth asking your tutor or a qualified scholar to look at the specific paperwork before you sign.
lessons.contracts__salam-istisna:
The general rule in trade is simple: you can't sell what you don't have. But two structures are recognized exceptions, both built to solve a real problem for producers who need capital before they have goods to sell.

**Salam** is a forward-purchase contract. The buyer pays the full price now; the seller delivers the goods later, on a set date. The conditions are spelled out plainly: whoever pays in advance must specify a known quantity, a known measure or weight, and a known delivery date. The goods have to be described by standard, replaceable specifications — "500kg of grade-A wheat" — not a one-of-a-kind item that can't be substituted. And the payment must be handed over in full, immediately. If it isn't, you end up trading one debt for another, which isn't allowed.

Why bother with this at all? Think of a farmer who needs cash in spring for seed and equipment, but won't have a harvest to sell until fall. Salam lets a buyer pay him now, at a price below what the crop will likely fetch later — in exchange for taking on the risk that the harvest could fail or the market price could drop. Both sides carry real risk. Nobody's just collecting interest on a loan.

**Istisna** is a manufacturing order — you're commissioning something that doesn't exist yet: a house, a piece of machinery, a custom production run. It differs from salam in two ways:

- Payment can be released in installments, tied to milestones or stages of work, instead of paid in full upfront.
- The delivery timeline is more flexible — what matters most is that the item and its specifications are pinned down precisely.

This is why istisna shows up in construction and project financing: a client pays as stages complete, a contractor builds to an agreed spec, and both sides are tied to actual production rather than to a debt changing hands.

What both contracts share is this: the thing being sold must be described precisely enough that if a dispute arises over whether it matches the order, there's a clear way to settle it. That precision in description is exactly how gharar — the uncertainty covered earlier in this module — gets removed from the deal.
lessons.contracts__why-contract:
The word "halal" printed on a product proves nothing by itself. What actually matters is the structure of the contract underneath it, and that structure gets checked with one question: who carries the risk.

Three prohibitions generate everything else. Riba is profit taken without risk, produced simply by the passage of a debt. Gharar is excessive uncertainty — the item, the price, or the timing isn't clear, so the parties are effectively buying a cat in a sack. Maysir is betting on an outcome, where one side's gain is directly the other side's loss.

A few practical rules follow from this.

You cannot sell what you do not own. The seller has to actually hold the item and carry the risk of owning it — if it's destroyed before delivery, that loss is the seller's, not the buyer's. This is exactly why Islamic financing structures transactions around buying and selling real assets rather than simply handing over cash and charging for its use.

The item and the price have to be defined. The longest verse in the Quran is entirely devoted to recording a debt in writing, with witnesses and a fixed term. Uncertainty isn't a minor detail here — removing it is treated as important enough to deserve its own dedicated instruction.

Honesty matters more than profit. A hadith states that both parties to a deal may cancel it as long as they haven't yet parted ways; if they were truthful and disclosed everything, their transaction is blessed — if they lied and concealed something, that blessing is destroyed.

Conditions agreed between the parties are binding. Muslims are bound by the terms they set — whatever is written into the contract is what gets honored.

So when you're looking at any financial product — a mortgage structure, a business financing arrangement, a savings product — don't start with its name. Ask three things instead: what exactly was sold, who owned it and at what point, and who eats the loss if it's destroyed. The answers tell you more than any label on the front page ever will.
lessons.halal-income__crypto:
There's no single ruling on cryptocurrency, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Scholars disagree, and the disagreement is substantive, not a technicality.

Those who permit it argue that in fiqh, "maal" (property) is anything with recognized value and usefulness — a digital asset that people accept and exchange fits that definition. Buying and selling it for immediate settlement is, in this view, no different from exchanging one currency for another.

Those who prohibit it argue the asset has no intrinsic value or backing, its price is driven by market sentiment rather than production, the volatility amounts to gharar (excessive uncertainty), and the dominance of speculative trading over real use amounts to maysir (gambling).

The middle position — arguably the most useful one for you — separates the instrument itself from how it's used. The debate over the asset's nature can continue, but a number of operations fall under well-known prohibitions regardless of how you classify the asset.

Here's what can be said without settling that debate:

- A fixed return promised in advance for lending your funds — staking or "lending" products with a guaranteed annual percentage — is a markup on debt, i.e. riba, no matter what asset is involved.
- Leveraged trading, futures, and options carry gharar and maysir: you're betting on an outcome, not participating in real exchange.
- A project whose actual business is gambling, indecency, or interest-based lending is screened out by its activity, exactly like any ordinary company would be.
- If you hold cryptocurrency as savings, it's included in your zakat calculation at market value on the date you calculate — this is the position of scholars who treat it as property.

This is directly relevant to how AM Network operates. We deliberately don't issue our own speculative token, even though that's the easiest way to raise money for a crypto project. The reason is gharar and maysir: a token whose price depends on expectations has undetermined value, and one holder's gain comes out of another holder's pocket. Our revenue instead comes as ujrah — a stated fee for a service rendered, 1 to 2.5% per transaction. We use the blockchain as a ledger where every record can be verified, not as a way to issue an asset.

One thing worth saying plainly: if you hold cryptocurrency, this is worth discussing with a knowledgeable scholar rather than settling by reading an article. We can show you where the boundaries are clear-cut. The dispute over the asset itself isn't ours to resolve for you.
lessons.halal-income__halal-basics:
Whether income is halal isn't decided by the amount on your payslip or the prestige of your job title. It comes down to three checks: what you're selling, how you got paid, and what the contract actually says.

**The thing itself.** If the product or service is forbidden, nothing about how professionally you handle it changes that. Selling alcohol, running a betting operation, distributing indecent content — competence and good customer service don't fix a forbidden core business.

**The method.** The general rule is that people may not consume each other's wealth unjustly — trade by mutual consent is the exception carved out. So even when the product is fine, the money becomes tainted if it was obtained through short-weighing, hiding a defect from a buyer, taking what belongs to someone else, or a bribe to grease a deal. A halal product sold through a dishonest method still produces impermissible earnings.

**The contract.** A fully permissible item can still be sold in a forbidden way — through interest, through a deal so vague neither side really knows what they're getting, or through terms where one party's gain is structurally the other party's loss. This is worth checking on financing arrangements, business partnerships, and investment products specifically, since the product being sold (a house, a share, a service) can be fine while the contract wrapped around it isn't.

Between the clearly allowed and the clearly forbidden sits a grey zone. The Prophet ﷺ described it directly: the lawful is clear, the unlawful is clear, and between them are unclear matters that many people don't recognize. Whoever stays away from the unclear protects his religion and his integrity. This isn't a call to be paranoid about every transaction — it's a practical rule for exactly the situation you'll actually face: you're not sure, so you find out before you commit, rather than assuming it's fine and sorting it out later.

Why bother, especially when you're busy running a household and a business. One hadith paints a traveler, worn out from the road, hands raised in prayer — but his food, drink, and clothing were all obtained through forbidden means. The question posed is blunt: how could such a prayer be answered? The point is that where the money comes from doesn't stay confined to the transaction. It follows the earner.

And there's a warning that reads like it was written for right now: a time will come when people stop caring whether their wealth came from the lawful or the unlawful. Staying attentive to the source of your income — your salary, your business revenue, your savings — is exactly what's being asked of you here.
lessons.halal-income__savings-takaful:
Commercial insurance draws objections from scholars on three separate grounds, not just one.

First, gharar — excessive uncertainty. You pay a fixed premium for an outcome that isn't fixed: pay into a policy for twenty years and get nothing, or pay one installment and receive a large payout. Second, maysir — gambling. The outcome hinges on an event, and one side's gain is the other side's loss. Third, riba — the reserves insurers collect are typically invested at interest.

Takaful is structured differently, and the difference isn't cosmetic — it's about who actually owns the money. Participants contribute to a shared fund as a mutual donation, not as payment for a service. Claims are paid out of that fund. The operating company never owns the fund; it manages it, earning either an agreed management fee or a share of investment profit. If a surplus remains at the end of a period, it goes back to participants or rolls forward — it doesn't become the operator's profit.

The core distinction: in commercial insurance, you and the insurer are two parties to a deal with opposing interests. In takaful, you and the other participants are partners helping each other, and the operator is just a hired manager. The Quran's instruction to cooperate in righteousness is the principle the model is built on.

Worth being honest about: takaful is a modern scholarly effort from the twentieth century, not something handed down directly in the texts. Different companies implement it differently, so check the actual contract rather than assume.

A separate case is insurance mandated by law — car insurance, health coverage required where you live. Scholars treat this separately, under the principle of necessity, and many don't consider a person sinful for what the law obligates and they cannot avoid.

On savings, briefly — for someone juggling salary, mortgage, and business inventory, this matters daily:

- Permitted: an interest-free checking account, a profit-sharing account under a mudaraba structure, physical gold and silver, or a stake in a real business.
- Not permitted: an interest-bearing deposit, regardless of what the bank calls it.

And remember: savings held in any permitted form still count toward your zakat calculation for the household.
lessons.halal-income__screening:
When you buy a share, you're buying a slice of a real business — and you inherit responsibility for what that business actually does. Checking a stock before you buy it works on two levels.

**Level one: what does the company do?** Some businesses are disqualified outright, regardless of their financials — making or selling alcohol, pork, tobacco, gambling and lotteries, indecent content, and interest-based banks or commercial insurers, since their core income is structurally built on riba.

**Level two: how clean are the finances?** Almost every large company holds interest-bearing cash or carries debt somewhere. Fully clean companies are rare, so modern standards set tolerance limits instead of demanding zero. AAOIFI Standard No. 21, for example, uses three checks:

- interest-bearing debt below 30% of market capitalization
- interest-bearing investments/deposits below 30%
- income from impermissible activity below 5% of total revenue

Two honest points here. First, this is a modern industry standard produced by specialist scholars — not a revealed text. Second, providers calculate differently: some use market cap as the denominator, others use total assets, and thresholds vary too. The same company can pass one screening service and fail another. That's not a mistake on anyone's part — it's two different careful methodologies, not one right answer and one wrong one.

**Purifying the income.** If a company has a small amount of impermissible income within the allowed limits, the matching slice of your dividends or capital gain isn't really yours to keep. You calculate that portion and give it away for public benefit — not as charity you're rewarded for, but as a cleaning of your wealth.

**And for zakat purposes:** shares you hold as an investment are included in your zakat calculation, but how depends on why you hold them. Shares bought to be resold are counted at full market value. Shares held for their dividends are counted, according to many scholars, by your proportional share of the company's current (liquid) assets rather than the full share price.
lessons.riba__riba-today:
The test is always the same: is the extra charge tied to time — how long money is used — rather than to a product, labor, or shared risk? Wherever you find that, you've found riba. Walk through your own financial life with this lens.

Credit card. Having the card itself isn't riba. It only appears if interest gets charged on a balance you didn't pay off. Clear the full balance in the interest-free period, and no riba occurs on that transaction — though scholars differ on how to view a contract that has interest built into its terms even if you never end up paying it.

Personal loans and car loans with interest. Straightforward riba: you return more than you borrowed, and the extra is simply the price of time.

Savings account with interest. Same riba, just from the other side — your deposit is a debt the bank owes you, and the interest is the markup on that debt.

Installment purchases. This one needs care. If a seller sets one fixed price for paying over time — say, a higher price than the cash price, but locked in at the contract's signing and never changing — most scholars treat this as ordinary, permissible trade: a price for a product with delayed payment, not a price for time itself. But if the amount grows because of a late payment, or interest accrues on the remaining balance, that's riba.

Mortgages. A standard interest-based mortgage falls under the prohibition of riba. Where it gets genuinely difficult is for Muslims living in places where Islamic mortgage products aren't available — scholars are recognized to differ here, some permitting a conventional mortgage under real necessity with no alternative, others not permitting it. This isn't something to settle from an article. If you're weighing a home loan, take your specific situation to a knowledgeable scholar rather than a general rule.

Late fees. If the penalty is a percentage that grows the longer you're late, that's riba. A fixed, one-time charge meant to cover actual administrative cost is judged differently by scholars.

If you run a business with inventory or manage family savings, apply the same question to every account and every contract you hold: is any part of this extra amount charged simply for time passing? If yes, it needs to go. If the extra is tied to a product's price or a service actually performed, it's likely just trade — but check the specifics rather than assuming.
lessons.riba__two-kinds:
Riba comes in two forms, and mixing them up leads to confusion about what's actually forbidden.

**Riba of debt** is the one everyone recognizes: a charge for using someone else's money or for delaying payment. This covers loan interest, interest accruing on a credit card balance, returns from an interest-bearing deposit, and late fees that grow with each day of delinquency. If you're carrying a mortgage or business credit, this is the category to check first.

**Riba of exchange** is less obvious. It shows up when you trade like-for-like items in unequal amounts, or with delay. A well-known hadith names six items — gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates, and salt — and sets the rule: if you're exchanging one for the other of the same kind, it must be equal amount for equal amount, and handed over on the spot. You can't trade 10 grams of gold for 12 grams of gold even if the quality differs — you'd need to sell one for cash, then use that cash to buy the other.

The practical case people miss: currency exchange. Swapping one currency for another is allowed at the going rate, but settlement has to happen immediately — both sides receive their side of the deal within the same transaction. If the payment on either end is deferred, you've stepped into riba, even though it looks like an ordinary money-changing transaction.

Riba of exchange can feel abstract — most people aren't trading gold bars — but it's the reason Islamic financial institutions structure their products around buying and selling an actual asset rather than simply lending money and charging for its use. Understanding this helps explain why a "profit-based" Islamic mortgage or financing product is built the way it is, instead of just being a renamed interest loan.
lessons.riba__way-out:
Finding out that part of your finances is tangled up in riba isn't a verdict — it's a starting point. The Quran speaks directly to people in exactly this position: give up what remains of the interest, meaning stop what's ongoing. The instruction is about the road ahead, not despair over the past.

Here's the order that actually works, especially when you're juggling a mortgage, business cash flow, and a household budget.

**Stop the inflow first.** No new interest-based loans, no new cards that accrue interest, no new interest-bearing deposits. If money keeps flowing in through the same channel, paying down the old balance is treading water.

**Get the full picture on paper.** List every obligation: where, how much, what rate, what term. This takes an hour, maybe two — but most people who feel stuck have never actually written it down. Not knowing the real number is often what keeps people frozen.

**Pay off the highest rate first**, not the largest balance or the one that feels most urgent emotionally. This is just arithmetic: the higher the rate, the faster it compounds, and the more you'll end up paying in interest if you leave it for last. If your mortgage carries a lower rate than a business loan or credit line, the business debt likely comes first.

**Deal separately with interest you've already received** — say, on a savings account. Scholars broadly agree you shouldn't keep this for yourself or spend it on personal needs. The common view is to give it away for public benefit, without seeking reward for it, since this is purification of wealth rather than charity in the usual sense. The exact method is worth confirming with someone knowledgeable rather than guessing.

**Don't sort this out alone.** A mortgage, an inheritance with interest attached, a business with partial interest financing — these are different situations, and a general rule can't replace someone looking at your specific numbers. Find a scholar who will actually go through the details with you.

One last thing worth saying plainly: fear and embarrassment are what make people put this conversation off for years, while the debt keeps growing in the meantime. Facing it early is always lighter than facing it late.
lessons.riba__what-is-riba:
Riba is an increase agreed in advance that you earn not from work, not from risk, and not from a real good or service — but simply from lending money or trading unequal for unequal.

The clearest example: you lend 1000 and demand 1100 back. That extra 100 is riba. It doesn't matter what you call it — interest, a "service fee," a charge for delay. What matters is where the increase comes from: the debt itself, not trade or shared risk. This is directly relevant if you're comparing a conventional mortgage to an Islamic financing structure, or deciding how to price a loan to a supplier or relative.

Why the prohibition is so strict: the increase in riba comes with zero risk to the lender. In a normal business deal, the seller carries real risk — the goods might not sell, might spoil, might drop in value. In riba, none of that applies. The lender gets their fixed cut regardless of whether the borrower's business succeeds or fails, even if the borrower is ruined. Profit with no risk shifts the entire burden onto the weaker side, and money keeps flowing from people who need it to people who already have plenty.

The prohibition isn't limited to whoever pockets the profit. A hadith names five parties as equally implicated: the one who takes the riba, the one who pays it, the one who writes up the contract, and the two witnesses. So sitting on the paperwork of an interest-based deal — signing as a witness, drafting the contract — falls under the same ruling as taking the money itself. Worth remembering if you're ever asked to co-sign or witness a loan agreement for someone else.

To be precise about what's actually forbidden: it's the increase charged for the debt itself. Profit from honest trade, from renting out property or equipment, from a joint investment where both sides share the risk — all of that is allowed, and encouraged. The issue was never profit itself. It's profit taken without risk, off the back of someone else's need — whether that's a friend short on cash, a customer buying on credit, or a business you're financing.
lessons.zakat-basics__eight-categories:
The Quran names exactly eight categories of zakat recipients. This isn't a suggested list — it's a closed set. Your zakat can only go to one of these:

- **The poor** (al-fuqara) — people whose money doesn't cover basic needs.
- **The destitute** (al-masakin) — an even harder situation than the above.
- **Zakat administrators** — people whose job is collecting and distributing it; they're paid from the fund itself.
- **Those whose hearts are to be reconciled** — including new Muslims going through a hard stretch.
- **Freeing people from bondage** — historically freeing slaves or captives; scholars today extend this to freeing people from modern forms of servitude.
- **Those in debt** (al-gharimin) — people who genuinely can't pay what they owe.
- **In the path of Allah** — scholars differ on how broadly to read this one.
- **The stranded traveler** (ibn as-sabil) — someone out of money on a journey, even if they're well-off back home.

That's the full list. Nothing outside it qualifies, no matter how good the cause sounds.

Who you can't give zakat to:

- Anyone you're already responsible for supporting — parents, children, your spouse.
- Anyone financially secure who doesn't fit one of the eight categories above.
- Most scholars hold that descendants of the Prophet ﷺ's family (Banu Hashim) are excluded from receiving zakat.

Here's the part that matters for someone juggling a household budget: other relatives — a brother, sister, uncle, cousin — are not off-limits. If they're in need and you're not already obligated to support them, giving them zakat is actually preferred over giving to a stranger. It does double duty: fulfilling the obligation and strengthening family ties at the same time. So before sending your zakat to an organization, it's worth asking whether someone in your own extended family qualifies.

This eight-category list is also the backbone of how AM Network evaluates who receives funds — the system checks a person's situation against these Quranic categories, while an actual person on the ground (an imam, a volunteer, or someone from a partner organization) confirms the need is real.
lessons.zakat-basics__nisab:
Nisab is the cutoff. Below it, no zakat is due at all — the system is designed to tax surplus wealth, not to squeeze people who are already stretched thin covering a mortgage, payroll, or family expenses.

The threshold is fixed in two metals: 85 grams of gold or 595 grams of silver. You take the current market price of the metal and convert that into your own currency — which is why the exact number changes year to year, and why it's worth recalculating rather than reusing last year's figure.

There's a real difference of opinion here worth knowing about, not glossing over: gold and silver nisab produce noticeably different amounts, with silver currently far lower. Some scholars calculate by gold, others by silver. Many contemporary scholars and zakat funds favor the silver threshold specifically because it's lower — more people end up obligated, and more support reaches those who need it. Neither side is "wrong"; it's a recognized scholarly difference, so check which standard your fund or scholar uses and be consistent with it.

The second condition is hawl: the wealth has to stay in your possession for a full lunar year (about 354 days). The clock starts the day you first hit nisab. For a household juggling salary, savings, and business inventory, balances naturally fluctuate — if your total dips below nisab mid-year but climbs back above it by year's end, most scholars say the clock does not reset. What matters is your position at the start and end of the period, not every point in between.

Practically, this means: pick one date on the lunar calendar and calculate on that same date every year. Many people choose Ramadan simply because it's easy to remember — but any fixed date works, as long as you're consistent so hawl is tracked properly across your combined assets (salary savings, business stock, and family wealth together, not each counted separately on its own timeline).
lessons.zakat-basics__what-counts:
Zakat applies to wealth that grows or sits accumulated — not to everything you own. The quick test: is this asset working as capital or savings, or is it something you use to live and earn?

**Counts toward zakat:**

- Cash — in hand, in bank accounts, on cards, plus savings.
- Gold and silver in any form — bars, coins, jewelry.
- Business inventory bought for resale — valued at today's market price, not what you originally paid.
- Investments — stocks, business shares, digital assets.
- Money owed to you, if you genuinely expect to get it back.

**Does not count:**

- The home you live in and personal belongings — clothes, furniture, dishes.
- The car you drive.
- Tools and equipment you use to earn a living — a craftsman's machine, a programmer's computer, a taxi driver's car.
- The building and equipment of a business — only the merchandise sitting inside it is zakatable, not the shop itself.

Before you total everything up, subtract debts you're obligated to repay — most scholars say this means primarily debts that are currently due, not ones stretching years into the future. So if you have a mortgage, the portion due now (not the entire remaining loan) is what you deduct — this is worth clarifying with someone knowledgeable if your situation is complex.

One point genuinely differs between scholars: women's jewelry worn for personal use. The Hanafi school says zakat is due on gold and silver jewelry regardless of purpose. Other schools generally don't require it if the jewelry is worn in reasonable amounts rather than stored as savings. This is a long-standing, recognized difference of opinion — not something this lesson can settle for you. Pick the position you follow after checking with someone qualified.

For a household, the practical approach is to add up all zakatable assets across the family under one calculation — cash, savings, gold, business stock, expected returns — subtract due debts, and apply one flat rate to the result:

**2.5% of the total — one-fortieth.**

That's the whole formula. The work is mostly in correctly sorting what belongs in the total and what stays out of it.
lessons.zakat-basics__what-is-zakat:
Zakat is the third pillar of Islam — a duty, not a favor you choose to extend to someone poor. If your wealth crosses a set threshold, the money owed to the needy is already theirs by right. You're not being generous; you're handing over what isn't fully yours to keep.

The word itself carries two meanings: purification and growth. Paying it purifies what remains of your wealth, and it purifies you of stinginess and over-attachment to money.

For someone juggling a salary, a mortgage, business stock, and household savings, the distinction that matters most is this: zakat is calculated on accumulated wealth, not on income. Your paycheck isn't taxed the moment it lands in your account. What matters is what's left, untouched, sitting as savings after a full year has passed. You could have a high income and still owe nothing, if you spend it all and end the year below the threshold. Conversely, modest income with real savings above the threshold means zakat is due.

This is also what separates zakat from sadaqah (voluntary charity), and it's worth keeping the two straight since they get mixed up constantly:

- Zakat is obligatory, has a fixed rate — 2.5% of qualifying accumulated wealth — fixed conditions for who must pay, and a fixed circle of recipients set out in the Quran.
- Sadaqah is voluntary, has no set amount, can go to anyone, anytime.
- Skipping zakat when it's due is a sin. Skipping sadaqah is not.

For a household with mixed assets — savings, business inventory, mortgage payments — the practical calculation (which accounts count, how debts factor in, how to value stock) goes beyond what this lesson covers. That's a separate, more detailed lesson; for your specific numbers, it's worth checking with the tutor or a qualified scholar rather than guessing.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__sadaqah:
Садака — это шире, чем строчка в бюджете. Есть хадис, где сказано, что каждый сустав человека должен давать садаку каждый день, когда встаёт солнце, — и дальше идёт список, в котором нет ни слова о деньгах: рассудить справедливо между двумя людьми, помочь с тяжёлой поклажей, доброе слово, каждый шаг к молитве, убранное с дороги препятствие. Если в этом месяце денежный поток напряжённый — ипотека, товар на складе, семейные расходы, — это не значит, что вы выпали из садаки. Возможность остаётся всегда.

Когда же речь о деньгах, Коран даёт образ приумножения: тот, кто расходует на пути Аллаха, подобен зерну, давшему семь колосьев, а в каждом колосе — по сто зёрен. Это не гарантия конкретного результата, а указание на масштаб, с которым можно думать о пожертвовании — не как о потере из бюджета, а как о посеве.

Но есть и то, что обнуляет эффект. Коран прямо говорит: не делайте свои милостыни тщетными попрёками и обидой. Если вы помогли родственнику и потом напоминаете ему об этом при случае — садака как будто и не была дана. Это стоит держать в голове именно тем, кто помогает системно: коллегам, родне, сотрудникам — напоминание о добром деле уничтожает его ценность.

Отсюда предпочтение скрытности. Открытая садака хороша, если она вдохновляет других делать так же — например, в рамках сбора на благотворительность. Но скрытая, отданная напрямую бедным, лучше — она защищает достоинство берущего и чистоту намерения дающего. Для человека с устойчивым доходом это практичный ориентир: то, что идёт близким или знакомым в нужде, разумнее отдавать без огласки.

Отдельная категория — садака джария, непрерывная садака. В хадисе сказано, что после смерти дела человека прекращаются, кроме трёх: непрерывной садаки, знания, которым продолжают пользоваться, и праведного ребёнка, который молится за него. Это меняет расчёт: разовая помощь закрывает сегодняшнюю нужду, а вложение, которое продолжает работать — колодец, книга, обученный человек, инструмент, приносящий пользу, — отдаёт и без вашего участия. Именно из этой идеи вырос вакф — механизм, о котором пойдёт следующий урок.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__three-forms:
Three ways money leaves your hand, and they work differently.

Zakat is mandatory. The rate is fixed at 2.5% of savings that have sat above the nisab threshold for a full lunar year. Who can receive it is fixed too — the Quran names eight categories, and you don't get to expand that list to, say, a school fundraiser you like or a relative's business idea. Once paid, the money is gone for good — it belongs to the recipient outright.

Sadaqa is voluntary. Any amount, any time, to anyone in need — and per many hadiths, sadaqa isn't even limited to money. Like zakat, once given, it's given; there's no getting it back.

Waqf is different in kind. You permanently remove the asset itself from circulation — the property, the building, the fund — it can never be sold, gifted, or inherited. Only what it produces gets distributed: rent, harvest, profit. If you put a house into waqf, you haven't given away the house — you've given away everything it will ever earn, forever.

Here's the rule that trips up people who are otherwise careful with their money: sadaqa never substitutes for zakat. You could give away ten times your zakat obligation over the year in charity — to your mosque, to relatives, to causes you believe in — and still owe zakat in full, if that giving was never actually designated as zakat, paid with the intention of zakat, to someone from the eight eligible categories. A voluntary payment, however generous, doesn't discharge a mandatory one. If you're running zakat calculations for a household — salary, business inventory, savings all mixed together — keep that 2.5% obligation tracked separately from your regular giving, not folded into it.

The reverse also matters: zakat is a floor, not a ceiling. The Quran says you won't reach true righteousness until you spend from what you love — and that's speaking about sadaqa, about what goes beyond the obligation. Paying your 2.5% checks a box; it isn't meant to be the whole story of your generosity.

One more thing worth holding in mind: the Quran sets riba and charity as opposite motions — Allah destroys the growth of interest and increases charity. Two ways wealth moves, pointed in opposite directions.

This lesson doesn't go into how to calculate nisab for mixed assets like business inventory alongside cash — if that's your situation, that's a question for the tutor or a qualified scholar.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__waqf:
Waqf started with an actual question, not a theory. Umar ibn al-Khattab came into possession of land in Khaybar — the best property he owned — and asked what to do with it. The answer he got: keep the land itself, and give away what it produces. Umar did exactly that, adding one condition: the land itself could never be sold, gifted, or inherited — only its yield would go out, to the poor, to relatives, to freeing people from bondage, and to travelers.

That's the entire mechanism, and it hasn't changed since. There's a body — the asset itself — and there's fruit — what it generates. The body is frozen permanently. The fruit gets distributed according to whatever purpose the founder named.

Over centuries this simple structure produced wells, free hospitals, libraries, travelers' lodges, even universities that ran themselves for hundreds of years without needing fresh donations each time. Not one-off charity, but self-sustaining institutions.

The founder's conditions aren't a suggestion. There's a governing principle that Muslims are bound by the conditions they set. If someone specified that the income go toward educating orphans, the person managing the waqf can't redirect it elsewhere — even if he genuinely believes the money would do more good somewhere else.

In practice today, a waqf can take the form of real estate, rental income, or a share in a business. There's also the separate question of a cash waqf — money placed into the waqf, invested, with only the return spent. A significant number of scholars, including in the Hanafi tradition, accept this, but there's no full agreement across the schools, so treat it as an open question rather than a settled one.

Here's why this connects to what's being built. Historically, waqf has broken down in the same place every time: the manager. Conditions get forgotten, property gets quietly sold, income drifts to the wrong recipients, and a hundred years later there's no way to check any of it. A smart contract is built for exactly the thing waqf requires — a condition that can be locked in so it can't be altered, and income that routes automatically without depending on anyone's good faith. Nothing here is live yet; the contracts are written but not deployed to the main network. But that specific property — not any enthusiasm for blockchain as such — is why this direction was chosen.
